tier_reason: Peer-reviewed NSDI'13 paper compares MemC3 against stock Memcached 1.4.13: full-system throughput 4.4 MOPS vs 1.5 MOPS (almost 3x, Fig. 9), 30% less memory for small key-value pairs, and a 5M/35M lookups/sec hash table. The CPU is stated (2x Xeon L5640), but the compiler and flags for the server builds are not, so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Full-system throughput over the network: MemC3 peaks at 4.4 MOPS vs 1.5 MOPS for original Memcached, 'almost 3x' (Fig. 9, 95% GET/5% SET YCSB Zipf workload). The paper says it uses 30% less memory for small key-value pairs, or stores 30% more objects; Table 3 shows cuckoo+CLOCK holding about 40% more 16B-key/32B-value items than Memcached's default chaining+LRU. The core cuckoo hash table alone does 5M lookups/sec per thread and 35M lookups/sec at 12 threads.
corrections.workload: End-to-end test: 95% GET/5% SET YCSB-generated Zipf workload, pre-generated as traces. It is sent from 50 client nodes over 10Gb Ethernet using libmemcached 1.0.7 multi-get (batches of 100 GETs) to MemC3 vs original Memcached 1.4.13, optimized Memcached, and sharded optimized Memcached. Each system gets 1GB of cache space. Separate local tests cover hash-table lookup throughput (single thread and multi-thread) and cache space efficiency and miss ratio (Table 3).
corrections.hardware: 2x Intel Xeon L5640 @2.27GHz (2x6 cores), 2x12MB L3 cache, 2x16GB DDR SDRAM, 10Gb Ethernet
corrections.caveats: The paper does not state the compiler or build flags for the MemC3/Memcached server builds; only the bench client Makefile shows gcc -std=gnu99 -O2. The end-to-end numbers use pre-generated YCSB traces, not live YCSB (the scripts are bench/ycsb_workload_gen.sh and bench/ycsb_workload_settings), with clients batching 100 GETs per multi-get. The server CPU is a low-power L5640. The only branch was last committed 2014-06-28 (repo pushed_at is 2017-04-28), and the project is unmaintained.

notes: The numbers in the record match the paper. The only fixes are that 'up to 3x' is 4.4 vs 1.5 MOPS ('almost 3x'), the paper lists DRAM as DDR SDRAM, not DDR3, and last_commit was the pushed_at date rather than the last commit on master (2014-06-28). License BSD-3-Clause, 156 stars, not archived, not a fork: all confirmed.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed NSDI'14 paper benchmarks MICA against Memcached, MemC3, Masstree and RAMCloud (Fig. 10, 13, 14) with the hardware stated. The netbench code and build flags (src/CMakeLists.txt) are in the repo, but the paper does not state the compiler version and the modified baseline versions are not published, so it is not A. The roughly 50-110x gap to Memcached exceeds the 50x cap threshold but is not implausible: it is against a peer-reviewed baseline that the paper shows peaks at 2 cores (Fig. 14), and the headline claim is 4-13.5x over the next-fastest system.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Tiny items (8B/8B), Fig. 10: MICA reaches 75.5-76.9 Mops on uniform and 65.6-70.5 Mops on skewed workloads. The next-best system (Masstree) tops out at 16.5 Mops; Memcached, MemC3 and RAMCloud stay at or below 6.1 Mops. Paper headline: 4-13.5x faster than the next fastest system, and 10.8x on skewed 50% GET. Against the custom Memcached (ported to MICA's kernel-bypass stack), which gets 0.7-1.3 Mops, MICA is roughly 50-110x faster on tiny items (derived from page data). Latency (Fig. 13, uniform 50% GET, tiny items) vs original kernel-stack Memcached: at a similar ~40 us latency MICA serves 69 Mops, 'more than two orders of magnitude faster than Memcached'. Original Memcached's latency is almost flat, while MICA's varies between 24 and 52 us depending on load.
corrections.workload: Network GET/PUT benchmark over UDP with MICA's DPDK kernel-bypass stack and no client-side batching. Item sizes: tiny (8B/8B), small (16B/64B) and large (128B/1024B). Key popularity is uniform or Zipf(0.99), at 50% and 95% GET. The server has 16 cores running 16 partitions (EREW). Compared against custom versions of Memcached (87e2f36), MemC3, Masstree and RAMCloud, all modified to use MICA's network stack, each run at its best core count. The latency test uses original Memcached with the kernel network stack.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The repo README requires gcc >= 4.6.0, and src/CMakeLists.txt sets -O9 -msse4.2 -march=corei7 -g.
corrections.caveats: The paper does not state the compiler version or build flags (flags appear only in the repo's CMake files), which is why this is capped at Tier B. The vs-Memcached/MemC3 throughput figures use custom versions of those systems ported to MICA's lightweight network stack, and those modified versions are not in this repo. The paper used DPDK 1.4.1 and the README requires DPDK >= 1.5.0, 2014-era APIs that will not build against modern DPDK without porting. The license (Apache-2.0) is asserted only in README text, with no LICENSE file. master was last committed 2014-03-03; the most recent commit anywhere is on the isca2015 branch (2016-01-18).

notes: The core throughput numbers match the paper; the vs-Memcached gap is actually much larger than the record's '>10x'. The workload's '8-partition' was wrong (the paper uses 16 partitions), and the latency clause 'more stable' was wrong (Memcached's latency is the flat one). last_commit 2016-01-18 is the isca2015 branch; the default branch is 2014-03-03; both are abandoned. 215 stars, gh license null, README Apache-2.0: all confirmed.

tier_reason: First-party cachelot.io chart compares Cachelot vs Memcached effective memory under a 2GB limit across four value-size datasets. The benchmark script (test/memory_consumption.py) is public, but no CPU, compiler, flags or Memcached version are stated, so it is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: The page says Cachelot 'keeps more items in the same amount of RAM than Memcached (saves up to 15% RAM, depending on the data and store patterns)', with 5-7% metadata overhead. The chart data (benchmarks.js, 2048MB budget, 10 runs) shows effective memory of 91.2-93.9% vs 79.5% for Memcached on small values (10B-1KB), 94.2-98.6% vs 86.7% on 1-4KB, 93.3-96.9% vs 87.2-87.3% on 4KB-1MB, and 93.4-97.4% vs 86.9-87.0% on mixed. That is up to about 14.4 points of the budget, or 7-18% more stored data (derived from page data). The README says Cachelot 'is faster in terms of latency' but gives no numbers.
corrections.workload: A Python script (test/memory_consumption.py) generates 2GB of random keys (10-60 chars) and values in four size ranges: 10B-1KB, 1-4KB, 4KB-1MB, and 10B-1MB. It fills cachelotd and Memcached, each limited to 2GB, over 10 shuffled runs and measures 'effective memory', the total bytes of surviving keys and values.
corrections.caveats: No CPU model, compiler, flags or Memcached version are stated for the vs-Memcached test. It measures memory efficiency only; the latency claim has no numbers, and a memslap throughput script (src/benchmark/memslap_benchmark.sh) exists with no published results. The current script's MEMORY_LIMIT is 4GB while the page reports 2GB runs. There is no independent verification. The last commit on master was 2023-04-12 (pushed_at 2024-08-07 is not a commit), over 3 years ago.

notes: The page shows a real vs-Memcached memory comparison. The '15%' is the page's own 'saves up to 15% RAM' wording, not 'more usable data'; the chart implies 7-18% more stored bytes. last_commit was the pushed_at date; the real last commit is 2023-04-12, which makes the project abandoned rather than stale. BSD-2-Clause and 376 stars confirmed.
